```{.julia .code-overflow-scroll}
using ComposableRecurrences

# Generation interval, lag 1 first: weights on y[t-1], y[t-2], y[t-3]
g = [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]
# Two strata mixed by a contact matrix
K = [0.9 0.1; 0.2 0.8]
infections = Recurrence(g; coupling = K)

# Reporting delay, lag 0 first: P(delay = 0, 1, 2, 3)
reports = Convolution([0.0, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2])

# Operators are callable. R_t is the gain, one column per day
R = fill(1.1, 2, 10)
y = infections(R; history = ones(2, 3))
cases = reports(y)

# Stop, keep the state, and resume for a forecast
y1, state = infections(R[:, 1:5]; history = ones(2, 3),
    return_state = true)
y2 = infections(R[:, 6:end]; history = state)
y ≈ hcat(y1, y2)
```

:::
:::

:::

The example runs on the main branch of [ComposableRecurrences.jl](https://github.com/EpiAware/ComposableRecurrences.jl).
The package is not registered yet, so install it from the repository to try it.

## The approach

Renewal processes, random walks, autoregressions and reporting delays share one structure.
Each step reads a window of past values, weights it by a kernel, and produces the next value.
This approach builds all of them from two operators rather than one bespoke loop per model.

A `Recurrence` feeds its output back into its own history.
At each step it convolves the last `L` values with its kernel, mixes strata through a coupling, scales by a gain, adds an input, and passes the result through a tuple of modifiers.
A renewal process is a `Recurrence` with the generation interval as kernel and `R_t` as gain.
A random walk is a `Recurrence([1.0])` with the noise as the added input.

A `Convolution` has no feedback.
It weights current and past inputs by a kernel, which covers reporting delays, moving averages and occupancy.

The package has no epidemiological assumptions.
It takes numbers in (kernels, gains, histories) and returns series out.
Modelling packages build their own named steps on top.

### Lag-first kernels, callable operators

Every kernel is written lag first, the way a generation interval or AR coefficients are written down.
A `Recurrence` kernel starts at lag 1 and a `Convolution` kernel at lag 0, so nothing is ever reversed by hand.
Operators are built once, outside the model, and called with the per-day inputs that are usually sampled.
Chaining is function composition, as in `reports(infections(R; history))`.

### Strata, time variation and coupling

Wrappers name the extra axis of a coefficient.
`PerStratum` gives each stratum its own kernel, `TimeVarying` lets a kernel or coupling change by day, and `Pairwise` gives each pair of strata its own lag kernel.
The coupling mixes strata before the gain, as a contact or mobility matrix does.
Couplings can be dense, sparse or diagonal matrices, and any real element type is accepted, so `Float32` and dual numbers pass through.

### Modifiers

Modifiers are applied in order after each step and carry their own state.
They handle what the linear core cannot, such as susceptible depletion or moving cases between strata.
A modifier is a plain type with an `apply!` method, so a modelling package can add its own.

### Plug-in adjoints

Reverse-mode AD is slow when each step copies its lag window into a new state.
The operators own a history buffer instead, which avoids that copy.
Native adjoints will plug in per operator, modifier or coupling by adding a method, with no AD declarations from the user.
`NoAdjoint(op)` turns an adjoint off, so its gain can be timed and the adjoint dropped if a backend catches up.
A [benchmark script](https://github.com/EpiAware/ComposableRecurrences.jl/blob/main/benchmark/gradients.jl) in the repository times plain AD gradients of the operators under Mooncake and Enzyme.

### How it fits with the other approaches

[Composable Turing models](composable-turing-models.qmd) will build on these operators.
Its renewal, delay and latent process steps become calls to `Recurrence` and `Convolution`, with the priors and observation models staying in the Turing layer.
The [composed distributions](composed-distributions.qmd) stack supplies the delay pmfs that become `Convolution` kernels.
The operators have no dependency on either, so they can also be used in other models.

The package has no runtime dependency on any other EpiAware package.
Today ComposableTuringIDModels runs its own renewal, delay and latent process loops.
Moving them onto one set of operators gives one forward kernel and one adjoint to maintain and test.

## Status

This approach is under development.
The core operators are merged on the main branch of ComposableRecurrences.jl.
These are `Recurrence`, `Convolution`, the `TimeVarying`, `PerStratum` and `Pairwise` wrappers, and the coupling and modifier interfaces.
The test suite differentiates them with ForwardDiff, ReverseDiff, Mooncake and Enzyme through plain AD.
Use-case tests against copies of the ComposableTuringIDModels steps they will replace are written but not yet switched on.

The built-in modifiers (`Depletion`, `Imports`, `Redistribute`, `Clamp`) and the native Mooncake and Enzyme adjoints are in progress.
A first registered release follows them, and then the port of ComposableTuringIDModels onto the operators.
An FFT method for long fixed kernels and a Reactant backend are later extensions.

## Where next

- The [ComposableRecurrences.jl repository](https://github.com/EpiAware/ComposableRecurrences.jl)
  tracks development, and its documentation will follow the first release.
- Building a full model with priors and observations? See the
  [composable Turing models approach](composable-turing-models.qmd).
- Need the delay distributions that feed a `Convolution`? See the
  [composed distributions approach](composed-distributions.qmd).
